### Research Report: Dark Chocolate and Stroke Risk

Your skepticism is well-founded based on current scientific literature. While some observational studies report a weak association between chocolate consumption and lower cardiovascular risk, systematic evaluations reveal major limitations:

* **Low Credibility of Evidence:** Comprehensive reviews note that observed inverse associations suffer from low certainty of evidence, potential residual confounding, and study biases, making it unwarranted to recommend dark chocolate for stroke or disease prevention (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-019-01914-9; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0261561418302048).
* **Inconsistent Findings:** Specific population analyses have found that chocolate intake is not significantly associated with stroke risk (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0021915017300941).
* **Extracts vs. Food:** Clinical trials investigating vascular health (such as the COSMOS trial) evaluate concentrated cocoa flavanol supplements rather than consumer dark chocolate, which contains calories, sugar, and fat (https://www.hcplive.com/view/cocoa-flavanols-supplement-lowers-risk-of-cardiovascular-death-study-finds).

### Conclusion
The claim that eating dark chocolate lowers stroke risk is **unproven**. Reported benefits stem primarily from weak observational data subject to lifestyle confounding, while clinical trial evidence relies on purified cocoa extracts rather than dietary dark chocolate.
